Hi Asha, Dylan —

Thanks for the initial details, Dylan. Based on the call notes and the preliminary workload sheet you shared (attached: Newcrest_ML_workload_profile.xlsx), here are our initial assumptions and a rough sizing sketch:

Assumptions (please correct if anything below is off):
- Production models: Large retrieval-augmented model (LAM) with 63k context; assistant model (ASM) at 8k context.
- Average response length: LAM 1,200 tokens; ASM 120 tokens.
- Peak 99th percentile concurrent request streams: 18 for LAM, 60 for ASM.
- KV cache usage: 40% of LAM requests reuse a long-lived prefix (session) and benefit from KV cache hit; remaining 60% are cold starts.
- Quantization target: test both int8 and 4-bit (QLoRA-like) at trial; prefer int8 stable, 4-bit for cost-sensitive troughs.

Key sizing notes:
1) KV cache memory scales with context * key/value sizes * number of concurrent sessions pinned to GPU. For your 63k window we estimate ~35–40 GB of KV memory per concurrent LAM session in float16. With int8/4-bit quantization at runtime (weights only), KV cache remains in fp16 by default unless we apply compressed KV formats — so KV remains one of the dominant factors.

2) Model weight memory (resident model shards) drops substantially with 8-bit or 4-bit quantization. Example: a ~80B-parameter LAM -> ~160 GB fp16 (sharded across GPUs); int8 quant -> ~85–90 GB; 4-bit -> ~50–55 GB. This reduces per-GPU model footprint and can change how many replicas we can place per node.

3) Practical pod design (initial recommendation):
- For predictable latency at the 99th, reserve 8xA100-80GB-equivalent GPUs dedicated to LAM traffic when running fp16 weights (baseline). That gives headroom for KV cache allocations and batching.
- With int8 quantization and KV caching aggressive reuse, we can target 5–6 GPUs (35–40% saving) but need to validate latency under tail workloads.
- With 4-bit, you may see up to ~2.5x compression vs fp16 on model weights, enabling ~3–4 GPU footprint, but KV cache still requires the same user-context memory unless we enable KV compression/offload.

I'll attach a one-page diagram of where KV and weight memory live (kv_cache_v2_diagram.png) and a spreadsheet with per-variant GPU math.

Next steps: Soojin will run two microbench scenarios (int8 steady state, 4-bit trial) against a representative 63k token synthetic session to validate latency and memory behavior.

—Marcus

Asha, Dylan, Marcus —

I ran the microbench plan this morning (attached results summarized in the spreadsheet). High-level findings and a recommended committed configuration: 

Summary of measured behavior (63k synthetic session test):
- fp16 weights, KV in GPU memory: p95 token latency = 85 ms, p99 = 210 ms (per-token decoding). End-to-end 63k flows frequently approach the 99th SLA boundary under concurrent load due to KV allocation spikes.
- int8 weights (runtime per-layer kernels optimized): model init & decode improved ~35% on throughput; p99 token latency ~150 ms. Memory reduced enough to place more replicas per node, lowering tail impact.
- 4-bit weights (experimental config with mixed kernels): throughput improved further but we saw occasional tail latency spikes tied to on-demand fp16 fallbacks during attention recalculation; quality metric (BLEU-style proxy) dropped ~0.9% relative to fp16 on our synthetic prompt set.

Sizing recommendation (Committed Dedicated Pool):
1) Baseline (fp16, conservative): 8 x A100-80GB equivalent GPUs dedicated to LAM, split across two physical nodes for failure domain. This supports 18 concurrent long-context streams with KV pinned on-GPU and meets your 99th tail target with a small buffer.
2) Mixed-int8 baseline: 6 x A100-80GB-equivalent GPUs with int8-optimized kernels. Keep 2 fp16 fallbacks reserved (hot standby replicas) to handle requests flagged by quality checks — this yields ~25–30% committed cost savings vs baseline.
3) Optional 4-bit trial pool: 4 x A100-80GB-equiv experimental pods with traffic routed via canary policy at 5% for 2 weeks. If quality and tail metrics remain within thresholds, consider moving additional capacity to 4-bit.

Operational controls we recommend including in the deal:
- Automatic per-request precision routing: requests failing quality checks or flagged by session metadata are routed to fp16 replicas.
- KV cache offload policy: cold sessions fall back to a lightweight CPU-backed remote KV tier (adds ~100–250ms latency for cold starts but saves persistent GPU KV memory).
- Canary & rollbacks: 5% traffic canary for any new quant profile for 14 days with automatic rollback triggers on quality regressions or p99 latency drift >10%.

Estimated committed pool and price delta (monthly):
- Baseline committed: 8 GPUs -> list price reference in attached pdf (redwood-dedicated-pricing.pdf).
- Int8 committed: 6 GPUs + 2 fp16 standby -> ~27% lower monthly compute than baseline.
- 4-bit trial: 4 GPUs experimental -> further savings but operational risk until validated.

I'll include these conservative math lines in the pricing deck and an ops runbook page for KMS integration and audit logs. Marcus will help write the short test harness for your QA team to run the quality checks we used.

—Soojin
